captions: Outside, your phone always knows where you are.
But step inside a big building,
and GPS goes quiet.
On our own campus,
new students and visitors can easily lose their way.
So we're building Indoor Nav for our college.
It gives you directions inside a building,
using just your phone,
in three simple steps:
pick, scan, and follow.
First, pick where you want to go.
Then scan the nearest marker.
It's just a printed sticker on the wall,
and the phone instantly knows where you are.
Now follow your route,
drawn on the building's own floor plan,
and worked out right on the phone.
If you need a route without stairs,
choose Step-free. If you would rather take the
stairs, choose Avoid lifts.
And when your route changes floors,
the app shows you exactly how you get
there, in 3D.
Clear steps guide you all the way to
the door. And if you take a wrong
turn, just scan any marker,
and your route starts again from there.
And in beta:
scan once, then simply walk,
with every turn read aloud.
Under the hood is a corrected,
bidirectional Dijkstra search.
Our first ESP32 version took a longer route
on 36 of 756 trips.
Today, every pair of places gets the shortest
route, and 192 automated tests keep it that way.
And it all works offline,
with no GPS,
no Wi-Fi, no beacons,
and no server.
Each block is set up from its own
floor plan, and shared as a single file.
Next, we want to map every block on
our campus, in one shared map library.
Beyond campus, it can help hospitals,
malls, airports, and exam halls.
And one day,
you could walk through a building once,
and let it map itself.
It started with a microcontroller and a cloud
database. Now, all it takes is a phone,
and a sticker.
Indoor Nav. Find your way, anywhere indoors.
